abstract: Dealers set limits on the largest position reached before a review horizon ends. Using hourly FX and weekly dealer positions, we compare conditional quantile forecasts with historical rules at matched history lengths and update schedules. Historical rules are demanding benchmarks. Long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in two periods. A calibration adjustment that updates after outcomes are observed retains the later gain (15.0\%), with 329 versus 328 breaches. Ranking against a shorter-history rolling rule changes across periods. On weekly aggregates, expanded regularization still leaves regression behind in 34 of 48 panel comparisons. Conservative short-sample validation also leaves large weekly losses. Lower scores accompany more breaches before calibration: 376 versus 360 in the matched FX comparison. These findings support selecting peak limits from accuracy, breaches and ranking stability together.
contributions:
The paper makes three empirical points.

\textit{First, matched FX gains recur across periods, and the later gain survives delayed calibration.} Regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% in the later and earlier periods (Table~\ref{tab:fx}). Calibration retains a 15.0\% gain with 329 versus 328 breaches. The shorter-history rolling reference reverses the earlier-period ranking.

\textit{Second, historical rules prevail across the weekly aggregate comparisons.} The Treasury-bill regression raises loss by 50.8\%, and expanded-menu regression still loses 34 of 48 additional-panel comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:weekly}). Conservative one-standard-error selection also leaves a worst-cell loss increase of 181.4\% in the earlier weekly period. More regularization and conservative validation therefore leave substantial observed gaps.

\textit{Third, lower quantile loss can coincide with more limit breaches.} The unwrapped matched FX gain comes with 376 versus 360 breaches (Table~\ref{tab:fx}). Elementary-score curves cross for both original main comparisons (Figures~\ref{fig:murphyfx} and~\ref{fig:murphybill}). Scores, error amounts and breach counts therefore provide complementary evidence for selecting a peak limit.
related: Relative to the endpoint and path-risk precedents in Table~\ref{tab:literature}, the contribution is three comparative findings. Third, the matched FX score gain accompanies 376 versus 360 breaches; the two original comparisons have crossing elementary-score curves (Table~\ref{tab:diagnostics}; Figures~\ref{fig:murphyfx}--\ref{fig:murphybill}). conclusion:
Simple historical rules are hard to beat when forecasting peak net positions in these records. Long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% across two periods. Calibration retains the later gain with 329 versus 328 breaches, while the shorter rolling reference changes the earlier ranking.

Weekly regression remains behind historical headroom: expanded regularization leaves 34 of 48 panel comparisons worse, and conservative validation leaves large losses. Lower pinball loss also accompanies more breaches before FX calibration (376 versus 360). Peak-limit selection should therefore assess accuracy, error amounts, breaches and reference stability together. The calibrated simulation leaves the hourly mechanism unresolved and fails to reproduce the persistent weekly losses; the empirical findings remain specific to the observed records.
cover_letter:
Dear Editors,

Long-history FX quantile regression lowers matched peak-position forecast loss by 14.8% and 16.6% across two periods, while historical rules prevail in most weekly comparisons.

Please consider "Hard to Beat: Historical Rules versus Conditional Quantile Models for Peak Net-Position Limits" for Journal of Forecasting. The paper addresses comparative forecast evaluation, demanding simple benchmarks and the practical choice of position limits. Its peak target requires completed forward labels and matched histories and update schedules.

The three empirical findings concern reference stability, weekly benchmark strength and score-breach disagreement. A calibration adjustment retains the later FX gain with 329 versus 328 breaches, but rankings against a shorter rolling reference vary by period. Expanded regression loses 34 of 48 weekly panel comparisons; conservative validation leaves large losses. Before calibration, the matched FX score gain accompanies 376 versus 360 breaches. Standard methods and elementary target properties support these comparisons; they are not presented as methodological contributions.

The submission includes the manuscript, Online Supplement, title-page template and code/results. The calibrated simulation preserves every adverse and numerically failed cell. Author information and all required declarations remain marked for author completion before submission.
